claims.text: A direct solid–liquid two-phase coexistence simulation can calculate melting properties of refractory materials within an ab initio framework.
The two-phase coexistence method is more computationally efficient than full free-energy thermodynamic integration.
The method can calculate melting temperature.
The method can calculate entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
The method can calculate volume change at the melting point.
A suitable simulation cell contains both a solid region and a liquid region of the same refractory material.
DFT-based molecular dynamics should be run near the expected melting point until steady-state phase coexistence is observed.
The coexisting solid–liquid interface mediates the phase transition and permits extraction of thermodynamic properties.
Dynamics at the solid–liquid interface determine equilibrium melting conditions.
The melting temperature can be identified under conditions where neither the solid nor liquid phase grows at the expense of the other.
Differences in energy between the solid and liquid phases can be used to compute latent heat and the enthalpy and entropy of fusion.
Differences in density or atomic packing between the phases can be used to compute the volume change on melting.
Predicted melting properties will agree with experimental values.
The computational cost will be much lower than that of complete free-energy integration across many state points.
Conventional ab initio thermodynamic integration using molecular dynamics is computationally expensive.
Finite-cell interfacial effects may limit the method's effectiveness.
Efficiency gains and quantitative accuracy may vary with system size and material complexity.
